steps.label: Conclusion (this suggests that)
steps.body: Producing characters more automatically frees up mental resources for other activities.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body:
Among 100 first-graders who got handwriting lessons, those whose composition skills had improved the most were the ones who had learned to write letters the most automatically.

Notice the mismatch: the composition half is about improvement, while the handwriting half is about how automatic the kids ended up.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
This is a study that hands us a correlation, and the author reads a cause into it.

CURIOUS FACT: Why were the kids with the biggest composition gains the same kids who wrote letters most automatically?

AUTHOR'S EXPLANATION: Handwriting lessons made writing automatic for some kids. Once forming letters stopped taking effort, those kids had attention left over for what they were writing, so their composition improved.

Now argue with it. How could we explain the same data without the author's story? Maybe some kids were simply stronger students from the start. They could already write letters automatically before the lessons, and they also picked up composition faster, with no help from automatic handwriting. The evidence doesn't rule that out, because it never tells us whether automaticity changed during the lessons.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body:
Strengthen answers for a curious fact usually do one of two things: make the author's explanation more plausible, or rule out an alternate explanation.

The best target here: show that the kids who gained the most automaticity during the lessons also gained the most in composition. Change tracking change is what we'd expect if automatic handwriting frees up attention, and it shrinks the room for the stronger-students-from-the-start story.

notes.body: This connects practice to automatic handwriting. That just tells us how kids became automatic. Composition never appears, so it does nothing to show that automatic writing frees up mental resources for other activities.

This one tempts because it links automatic writing with composition gains. But it is about kids who were already automatic before the lessons, and that fits both stories equally well: automatic writers had attention free, or they were simply stronger students who would improve at composition anyway. An answer that fits the rival as well as the author's story can't favor the author. B never shows that becoming more automatic did anything.

This is the prediction. The evidence only said the best improvers ended up most automatic. C says the kids whose automaticity improved more also generally improved more at composition. Now the gain in one skill tracks the gain in the other during the same lessons, which is what the author's story predicts and what the stronger-students story doesn't need.

The move: when a study's evidence compares a starting trait with an improvement, look for an answer that turns it into change matching change.

A representative group helps us apply the results to first-graders in general. It doesn't touch the real question, which is whether automatic handwriting causes the composition gains or something else explains both.

This runs the other way. Kids who started with strong composition skills became much more automatic, which hints that composition skill (or general ability) drives automaticity. That's a rival story, not support for the author's one.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: In northern Europe, archaeologists have discovered 400,000-year-old sharpened wooden poles alongside flint cutting implements and the remains of horses. It is normally assumed that Homo sapiens did not inhabit Europe prior to 200,000 years ago.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: This discovery [the sharpened poles, cutting implements, and remains] effectively disproves the widespread belief that the humanlike precursors of Homo sapiens were entirely gatherers and scavengers and did not hunt.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Start with who made the poles. If Homo sapiens weren't in Europe until 200,000 years ago, then the 400,000-year-old poles belonged to the humanlike precursors. The argument needs that part, and it gets it from the second premise.

The weak part is what the poles were for. The conclusion says the find disproves the belief that the precursors were only "gatherers and scavengers and did not hunt." That only works if the poles and flint were used to hunt.

How could we argue they weren't? Maybe the sharpened poles were for fending off predators. Maybe the horses died on their own, and the precursors used the flint and poles to cut up and carry away the carcasses. Either way, the find fits a group of scavengers just fine.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer that shows the poles were used for hunting, or one that rules out the non-hunting uses, such as defense or handling scavenged meat.

notes.body:
This rules out the two best scavenger stories. If the poles weren't for "self-defense" and weren't used to "cut or transport scavenged carcasses", hunting becomes the likeliest use for sharpened poles found next to horse remains. It doesn't prove the precursors hunted, but it closes the gap the argument left open.

The move: when the evidence is a set of objects and the conclusion is about what they were used for, strengthen by eliminating the other uses.

This says people in the area used stones and sticks as tools. The argument already assumes the precursors made the tools. The open question is what the tools were for, and B doesn't say anything about hunting.

C is about when Homo sapiens evolved, but the premise that matters is about when they lived in Europe, and evolving earlier doesn't put them in Europe earlier. If it did anything, it would open the possibility of Homo sapiens having made the poles, which hurts the argument. Either way, it says nothing about whether the poles were used to hunt.

Behavior that varied across ecosystems tells us nothing about what this group in northern Europe did. Divergent behavior could include hunting or not, so D gives us no reason to think these poles were hunting tools.

This is about Homo sapiens who already hunted, not about the precursors. Knowing that later hunters kept scavenging and gathering gives no evidence that the precursors hunted at all, which is what the conclusion needs.
